docs.title: The geostack
docs.text: Find the data, read it, cut it to size, compute on it — one composable stack. Six Python packages that interlock end to end, with the Operator / Sequential / Graph composition core supplied by pipekit.

docs.title: Where it comes from
docs.text:
If you have used xarray, you know split → apply → combine: group the data, run a function on each group, glue the results back together. A geospatial pipeline is the same idea with more steps on either side. Before you can split a scene you have to search an archive for it, catalog what you found so the next question is a query rather than a crawl, save (stage) only the files that matter, and stream them as lazy windows because the scene does not fit in memory. After you combine, you write a georeferenced result.

Two further stages are proposed and drawn dashed: commit the result as a version that appears all at once (#665), and publish a record of it to a product catalog, where the next search can find it (#671).

Most codebases rebuild that loop per project, so every step is hard-wired to the next. The geostack gives each step its own package and one small, typed seam between neighbours: a GeoSlice is the request every catalog answers, a geoarray.GeoArray is the array every reader returns and every operator takes, and a Patch is what the patcher hands an operator. Because operators are plain pipekit objects, the patcher itself becomes an operator — tile → predict → stitch is one more Sequential.

docs.title: The packages
docs.text:
Package Import Use it to… Docs geotoolz-ops geoops compute on rasters with carrier-preserving operators (radiometry, indices, masks, geometry, ML, …) Operators geotoolz-patcher geopatcher split a field into patches, run an operator per patch, stitch back (Geometry × Sampler × Window × Aggregation) Patcher geotoolz-catalog geocatalog find, index, join, load and stage files (GeoSlice queries over GeoParquet) Catalog geotoolz-cloud geocloud reach object storage: one client pool, file verbs, credentials, COG reads and writes Cloud geotoolz-products geoproducts read Earth-observation products (GOES-R ABI, Himawari AHI, Carbon Mapper, …) as geoarray.RasterSources that read GeoArrays Products geotoolz-array geoarray carry rasters: GeoArray (NumPy or JAX data with transform, CRS, fill and attrs; a JAX pytree), Grid / PixelWindow, the RasterSource protocol, the georeader bridge Array

Solid arrows are hard dependencies, dotted ones opt-in extras, and nothing points back up: install only the packages you need. How the packages interlock walks through every seam.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
pip install geotoolz                          # operators
pip install geotoolz-patcher                  # patcher
pip install geotoolz-catalog                  # catalog
pip install geotoolz-cloud                    # object storage, COG writes
pip install geotoolz-products                 # product readers
pip install geotoolz-array                    # the GeoArray carrier alone (`[jax]` for JAX)
To connect… Install operators ↔ patcher (geoops.patch_ops) geotoolz-ops[patch] catalog → patcher (geocatalog.patch.field_for) geotoolz-catalog[patch] catalog staging from buckets (geocatalog.staging.stage) geotoolz-catalog[cloud] catalog ← STAC searches (geocatalog.sources.from_stac_search) geotoolz-catalog[stac] patcher ↔ COGs in buckets (geopatcher.fields.CogField) geotoolz-patcher[cog] COG reads (geocloud.cog.CogSource) geotoolz-cloud[cog] a sensor's reader and its bucket helpers geotoolz-products[goes] / [himawari] / [carbonmapper] a sensor's presets as geotoolz operators geotoolz-products[operators]

Each package page lists its own extras. Pre-PyPI, install from a clone:

git clone https://github.com/jejjohnson/geotoolz && cd geotoolz
uv sync --all-packages --all-groups --all-extras

docs.title: Quickstart — catalog → patcher → operators
docs.text:
Summer-2024 NDVI over Lake Tahoe: discover Sentinel-2 L2A on the Planetary Computer, mosaic the red and near-infrared bands onto one grid, and run NDVI tile by tile with feathered seams. Every binding is typed and every array is annotated with its shape. It needs pip install 'geotoolz-ops[patch]' 'geotoolz-catalog[stac,cloud,patch]'.

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import planetary_computer
import pystac_client
from geoarray import GeoArray

import geocatalog as gc
import geopatcher as gp
import geoops as gz
from geoops.patch_ops import ApplyToChips, GridSampler, MergePatches

client: pystac_client.Client = pystac_client.Client.open(
    "https://planetarycomputer.microsoft.com/api/stac/v1",
    modifier=planetary_computer.sign_inplace,
)
aoi: gc.GeoSlice = gc.GeoSlice(
    bounds=(-120.25, 38.85, -119.85, 39.30),              # Lake Tahoe, lon/lat
    interval=pd.Interval(pd.Timestamp("2024-06-01"), pd.Timestamp("2024-09-30"), closed="both"),
    resolution=(0.0001, 0.0001),                          # ≈ 10 m → grid (H, W) = (4500, 4000)
    crs="EPSG:4326",
)

# 1 · find — one catalog per band, staged to local disk
bands: dict[str, gc.GeoCatalog] = {
    band: gc.staging.stage(
        gc.sources.from_stac_search(client, collections=["sentinel-2-l2a"], bounds=aoi.bounds,
                            datetime="2024-06-01/2024-09-30", asset_key=band),
        dest="./cache",
    )
    for band in ("B04", "B08")
}

# 2 · read — mosaic each band onto the AOI grid, stack red + NIR
red: gp.RasterField = gc.patch.field_for(bands["B04"].query(aoi), aoi)   # (1, 4500, 4000) uint16
nir: gp.RasterField = gc.patch.field_for(bands["B08"].query(aoi), aoi)   # (1, 4500, 4000) uint16
scene: GeoArray = gz.StackBands()([red.reader, nir.reader])         # (2, 4500, 4000) uint16

# 3 · cut + compute — 256² tiles, 64 px overlap, Hann-feathered seams
patcher: gp.SpatialPatcher = gp.SpatialPatcher(
    geometry=gp.spatial.geometry.Rectangular(size=(256, 256), boundary="pad"),
    sampler=gp.spatial.sampler.RegularStride(step=(192, 192)),
    window=gp.spatial.window.Hann(),
    aggregation=gp.spatial.aggregation.OverlapAdd(),
)
ndvi: gz.Sequential = gz.DNToReflectance(scale=1e-4) | gz.NDVI(red=0, nir=1)  # (2, h, w) → (h, w)
field: gp.RasterField = gp.RasterField(scene)
tiled: gz.Sequential = gz.Sequential([
    GridSampler(patcher=patcher),                        # field → list[Patch]       (2, 256, 256) each
    ApplyToChips(operator=ndvi),                         # list[Patch] → list[Patch] (256, 256) each
    MergePatches(aggregation=gp.spatial.aggregation.OverlapAdd(), domain=field.domain),
])
result: GeoArray = tiled(field)                        # (4500, 4000) float64 · NaN = no data

MergePatches places the chips on the domain's grid and keeps the band axes the chips carry, so NDVI's (h, w) chips merge into one (H, W) GeoArray on the scene's transform and CRS.

docs.title: Building with agents
docs.text: The stack is meant to be built on: your code should be the science, and the plumbing — discovery, indexing, reading, tiling, stitching, object storage — should come from these packages. Coding agents tend to re-implement what they cannot see, so the stack ships three things that let them find it.

docs.title: The capability index
docs.text: Capability index lists every public name in the six packages, once, at its home, with a one-line summary. It is regenerated from the code and checked in CI, so it never drifts. Point an agent at it before it writes a helper.

docs.title: The Claude Code plugin
docs.text:
The repository is a Claude Code plugin marketplace. In any project:

/plugin marketplace add jejjohnson/geotoolz
/plugin install geotoolz@geotoolz

The plugin adds:

  • build-geo-pipeline (skill) — loads whenever a task involves rasters, satellite imagery, STAC or tiling: which package does what, the canonical catalog → patcher → operators → write pipeline, the pipekit Operator and GeoArray contracts your own steps must keep, and the anti-patterns to avoid.
  • geostack-reuse-reviewer (subagent) — a read-only check of a diff for code that re-implements something the installed packages already provide.

docs.title: llms.txt
docs.text: For other agents and tools, the docs site serves llms.txt: a curated map of the stack and its key pages.

docs.title: Rules for your project's AGENTS.md
docs.text:
Paste this into the agent instructions of a project that builds on the stack:

## Geospatial code: build on the geotoolz stack

This project uses geoops (operators), geocatalog (find / index / load),
geopatcher (tile / stitch), geoproducts (EO product readers) and geocloud
(object storage). Before writing any raster, catalog, tiling, product-reading
or object-store helper, search the capability index
(https://jejjohnson.github.io/geotoolz/capabilities/) or the installed
packages' `__all__`, and compose what exists. New processing steps are
`pipekit_ops.Operator`s that keep the two contracts, so they chain with
`geoops.Sequential` and run in a `pipekit_ops.Graph`:

- **Operator.**
  - Implement `_apply`, never `__call__`.
  - Use a keyword-only constructor that holds configuration only (no
    rasters), so the auto-derived `get_config()` is JSON and
    `Operator.from_state(op.state)` round-trips.
  - Set `forbid_in_yaml` on live objects, and `_terminal` when the step
    returns a non-raster.
  - Use pipekit's `Retry` / `Try` / `Branch` / `Cache` / `ThreadMap`
    instead of writing your own.
- **GeoArray.**
  - Bands are on axis -3: `(C, H, W)` or `(T, C, H, W)`.
  - A GeoArray in returns a GeoArray on the same transform and CRS; a
    plain array in returns a plain array; the input is never mutated; a
    georeader `GeoTensor` is refused (convert it with
    `geoarray.interop.georeader.from_georeader`).
  - `attrs` are immutable; per-band keys match the output bands, and band
    names go under `band_names`.
  - `fill_value` is nodata: `False` for masks, `0` for labels, `NaN` for
    new floats.
  - Several rasters must share a grid; mask `True` means drop.
- Keep them with the helpers in `geoops.carrier` (`wrap_like`,
  `mask_invalid_to_nan`, `over_frames`, `resolve_band`, `require_grid_match`),
  and test every new step with `geoops.testing.check_operator(op, scene)`.

The build-geo-pipeline skill in the plugin below spells the contracts out, with a worked operator and a self-check.

docs.title: Upstream: pipekit_ops
docs.text:
The composition framework every operator subclasses. Use these instead of writing your own control flow, caching, observation, QC, parallel map or serialisation; a carrier-agnostic need belongs upstream, not here.

Name Kind What it does AssertCallable class Pass-through; raise QCError if predicate(x) is falsy. AssertDType class Pass-through; raise QCError if getattr(x, 'dtype') mismatches. AssertHasAttribute class Pass-through; raise QCError if attribute missing (or value mismatches). AssertShape class Pass-through; raise QCError if getattr(x, 'shape') mismatches. AssertSignature class Pass-through; raise QCError unless the carrier's dims fit pattern. AssertThat class Pass-through; raise QCError if pred(x) is falsy. Assoc class Add a key whose value is computed from the whole dict (toolz assoc). AsyncMap class Apply op to each item of an iterable inside an async event loop. BackendError class Inputs on more than one backend, or a backend the code does not run on. BatchedMap class Split an iterable into batches and call op on each batch as a list. Branch class Binary conditional: run if_true or if_false based on a predicate. Cache class Memoise an inner operator by hashing its input and the inner pipeline. Carrier class Re-exported from typing. CarryState class Base class for state threaded through a stateful pipeline. Coalesce class Try each source in order; return the first output that satisfies is_ok. Concat class Flatten exactly one level (toolz concat). ConfigMixin class Auto-derive get_config() from __init__ parameter names. Const class Return a fixed value, ignoring any input. Count class The number of items (toolz count). CountBy class Count items per key, in first-seen order (toolz countby). DirectoryStore class One file per key under root, written atomically. Dissoc class Drop some keys; missing keys are ignored (toolz dissoc). Failed class The slot of an item that failed under on_error="collect". Fanout class Apply each named operator to the same input; return a dict of outputs. Filter class Keep the items a predicate accepts (builtin filter). FittableTransformer class Anything with sklearn-style fit + transform methods. Fold class Associative fold over chunks, reduced in parallel through Map. Get class Index into a mapping or sequence (toolz get). GetIn class Walk a key path through nested containers (toolz get_in). Graph class A symbolic operator graph with multiple inputs and outputs. GroupBy class Group items by a key, in first-seen order (toolz groupby). Histogram class Controller that captures simple histograms by key. Identity class Explicit no-op. Returns its input unchanged. Input class A named entry point into a Graph. LabelledAdapter class An adapter that can set the labels of named dims (optional). Lambda class Wrap an arbitrary callable as an Operator. Log class Pass the carrier through and write one logging record per call. Map class Apply op to every item, on any executor, with a bounded window. MapError class Every failure of a Map(on_error="collect") run, with the partial results. Memoize class Memoise an inner operator by hashing its input and the inner pipeline. MemoryStore class A dict guarded by a lock: shared by the threads of one process. Merge class Union of several mappings; later inputs win (toolz merge). MissingAdapterError class A carrier from a known family arrived with no adapter registered. NamedArrayAdapter class What carrier-agnostic code needs from one carrier family. Node class A vertex in a Graph. Not class Negate a predicate; the operator form of complement. Operator class Base class for pipekit operators. PartitionAll class Split into tuples of n consecutive items (toolz partition_all). Pick class Keep only some keys, in the order given. Predictor class Anything with a sklearn-style predict method. Prefetch class Run op up to depth items ahead of the consumer, in input order. ProcessMap class Apply op to each item of an iterable using a process pool. Profile class Controller that records per-step wall-clock timings. QCError class Raised when a QC assertion fails. Subclass of AssertionError. Quarantine class Non-raising QC: on failure log and return sentinel; on success pass through. RateLimit class At most calls starts of op in any window of period seconds. Reduce class Left fold (functools.reduce), with the operator called on one pair. Remove class Drop the items a predicate accepts (toolz remove). Rename class Rename keys; unlisted keys pass through and the order is kept. Retry class Retry an operator on transient failures with exponential backoff. Sequential class Apply a list of operators in order, threading the output of each into the next. ShapeTrace class Log shape / dtype of each carrier passing through. Signature class Immutable shape + dtype record. Sink class Apply a side-effecting write and pass the input through unchanged. Snapshot class Controller that captures intermediate carriers by name. SortBy class A stable sort by key (builtin sorted). StatefulOperator class Marker base for operators whose _apply threads carry-state. Store class What Cache needs from a store: membership, load and save by key. Switch class Multi-way dispatch on key(carrier). Take class The first n items (toolz take), for dry runs. Tap class Fire a callback on the carrier; return the carrier unchanged. ThreadMap class Apply op to each item of an iterable using a thread pool. Timeout class Raise TimeoutError if op has not returned after seconds. Try class Run primary; on caught exceptions run fallback. Unique class The first occurrence of each item, or of each key (toolz unique). Until class Apply op until pred holds, at most max_iter times. UpdateIn class Replace the value at a key path by op(value) (toolz update_in). ValMap class Apply an operator to every value, keeping the keys (toolz valmap). Zip class Align several iterables into tuples (builtin zip), strict by default. allowed function Return the registered class names ("module.Class" keys). backend_name function "jax", "dask" or "numpy" for raw data (tracers count as JAX). backend_of function The backend of a carrier or a raw array; docs.title: Contributing
docs.text: This page documents the label taxonomy, epic model, and issue conventions used in this project.

docs.title: Label Taxonomy
docs.text:
Every issue carries exactly one type:*, one or more area:*, at most one layer:*, one wave:*, and one priority:*.

Scope Labels Type type:epic-wave, type:epic-theme, type:feature, type:design, type:chore, type:docs, type:bug, type:research Area area:engineering, area:testing, area:docs, area:code — extend per project (e.g. area:algorithmic, area:integration) Layer layer:0-primitives, layer:1-components, layer:2-models — only if the project has a formal layer stack Wave wave:0, wave:1, wave:2, … — release-scoped phases (add wave:N-<slug> variants for descriptive labels) Priority priority:p0 (blocker), priority:p1 (high), priority:p2 (normal)

Bootstrap the standard set on a fresh repo:

make gh-labels

The script lives at .github/scripts/create-labels.sh. Edit the hard-coded create … entries in the script to customise area:*, layer:*, and wave:* for the project, then re-run — the script is idempotent.

docs.title: Two-Layer Epic Model
docs.text:
Work is organised as Wave → Theme → Issue:

[EPIC] Wave N   (L1)   —   release-scoped mega-epic, owns a milestone
  ├── [EPIC] <theme>   (L2)   —   parallel-safe group of issues
  │     ├── feature / design / chore / bug issue
  │     └── …
  └── [EPIC] <theme>   (L2)
        └── …
  • Wave epic (type:epic-wave) maps one-to-one with a milestone (vX.Y-<slug>). Groups several Theme epics that can run in parallel.
  • Theme epic (type:epic-theme) groups concrete issues that ship together as a coherent slice. Themes inside a wave are parallel-safe unless the body says otherwise.
  • Issue (feature / design / chore / bug) is the leaf — a single substantial deliverable that rolls up to a Theme epic.

Stragglers are discouraged: any type:feature issue should attach to a Theme epic. If no suitable theme exists, create one first.

docs.title: Issue Format
docs.text:
Issue templates live in .github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/:

Template When to use Epic — Wave (L1) Opening a new release-scoped wave Epic — Theme (L2) Grouping related issues inside a wave Feature / Enhancement One substantial deliverable Design / ADR Resolve an open design question for a new API Bug report Something isn't working Research / Comparative Analysis Study prior art (external repo, paper) and produce a prioritized roadmap of follow-up issues

Feature + Design templates include two optional sections for context-heavy issues:

  • Design Snapshot — paste API sketches, code examples, or excerpts from private / external design docs so the issue is self-contained.
  • Mathematical Notes — equations, sign conventions, numerical considerations.

Delete either section if not relevant. Both exist so that an implementer (human or AI agent) can work on the issue without opening other repos or channels.

docs.title: Creating issues
docs.text: New issues should use one of the templates in .github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/ so that labels, required sections, and title conventions are consistent.

docs.title: From the UI
docs.text: Click New issue on the repo's Issues tab and pick a template. The body is pre-filled with the section scaffolding — fill in, apply labels and milestone, submit.

docs.title: From the CLI
docs.text:
For drafted content, write the body to a file (minus the template's YAML frontmatter), then:

gh issue create \
  --title "feat(primitives): diagonal BLR update step" \
  --body-file /tmp/issue-body.md \
  --label "type:feature,area:algorithmic,layer:0-primitives,wave:1,priority:p1" \
  --milestone "v0.1-diagonal"

To open the UI in a browser with a template pre-selected:

gh issue create --web

The web flow opens /issues/new/choose so you can pick the template in the UI. gh issue create does not support pre-selecting a template for the web path; the --template flag is only used as starting body text in the non-web flow.

After the issue is created, apply native parent / blocked-by links via the Makefile targets documented below in the Relationships section (or make gh-sub / make gh-block).

docs.title: From Claude Code
docs.text:
The create-gh-issue skill (at .claude/skills/create-gh-issue/SKILL.md) guides Claude through:

  • Picking the right template (decision tree covering feature / design / bug / research / epic-wave / epic-theme)
  • Drafting the body with required sections + rename guidance for optional sections (Design Snapshot → Demo To Implement, etc.)
  • Applying the correct label set (which type:* + area:* + layer:* + wave:* + priority:* combos are valid for each work type)
  • Setting the milestone (which vX.Y-<slug> corresponds to the wave)
  • Applying relationships (chains to link-gh-issues skill for native sub-issue + blocked-by links)
  • Style conventions — unicode math, text code fences, code-first-prose-last
  • Bulk workflow — publishing a .plans/<wave>-backlog.md file into real GitHub issues (multi-pass: wave epic → theme epics → leaf issues → relationships), with draft-ID → GH-number mapping

Example prompts:

  • "Open a feature issue for the diagonal BLR update step, child of theme epic #27"
  • "File a design issue for the per-parameter prior question"
  • "Publish the drafts in .plans/wave-1-backlog.md as real issues and wire up the sub-issue links"
  • "Open a research issue comparing pof vs this project, based on my notes in <path>"

docs.title: Drafting a wave backlog
docs.text:
For large planning exercises (new wave, new release, large refactor), draft the whole backlog as one markdown file before opening GitHub issues. A template lives at docs/templates/wave-backlog.md.

Why:

  • Review the whole wave in one scroll instead of clicking through 15 half-drafted issues
  • Share context once at the top (Shared Context · Design Snapshot · Intended Package Layout · Runtime Boundary) rather than duplicating across every child issue
  • Stable draft IDs (<PREFIX>-01, <PREFIX>-02, …) let child issues reference each other before GitHub issue numbers exist

Workflow:

  1. Copy docs/templates/wave-backlog.md into your project's .plans/ directory (gitignored). Rename to describe the wave — e.g. .plans/wave-1-backlog.md.
  2. Pick a short project prefix (e.g. PYX for pyrox, OBX for optax_bayes). Number drafts sequentially.
  3. Fill in shared context at the top, then draft each issue body.
  4. When the file is ready, open each draft as a real GitHub issue using the matching .github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/. Copy the body verbatim.
  5. Record GitHub issue numbers next to draft IDs in the backlog file, or replace draft IDs throughout. Update cross-references.
  6. Either delete the backlog file or archive it in .plans/archive/.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
Use an explicit ## Relationships block at the bottom of each issue / epic body:

## Relationships
- Parent: #<theme-epic>
- Blocked by: #
- Blocks: #
- Related: #

GitHub's task-list feature links bidirectionally from the parent, so checklist items in a Theme epic body auto-show in the referenced issues.

docs.title: Applying native GitHub relationships
docs.text:
The prose ## Relationships block above is a human-readable record. GitHub also exposes two native relationship features that power the UI sub-issue panel and the dependency graph — apply both:

Prose line Native feature Mutation Parent: / Theme Epics / Issues checklist Sub-issues (parent ↔ child hierarchy) addSubIssue / removeSubIssue Blocked by: Typed dependency addBlockedBy Blocks: Inverse — applied on the OTHER issue addBlockedBy (on the blocked side) Related: No native feature prose only

docs.title: From the UI
docs.text:
• Sub-issues — open the parent issue, side-panel → Sub-issues → Create sub-issue or Add existing sub-issue.
  • Blocked by — open the blocked issue, side-panel → Development → Mark as blocked by.

docs.title: From the CLI (Makefile targets)
docs.text:
For scripted work, the repo ships a helper script wrapped by three make targets:

# Link children as sub-issues under a parent
make gh-sub PARENT=7 CHILDREN="42 43 44"

# Mark issue 44 as blocked by 43
make gh-block ISSUE=44 BLOCKED_BY=43

# Inspect parent / sub-issues / blocking / blocked-by for an issue
make gh-show ISSUE=44

Direct script usage (same functionality plus unlink commands):

bash .github/scripts/link-issues.sh sub     <parent> <child> [<child> ...]
bash .github/scripts/link-issues.sh block   <issue> <blocker>
bash .github/scripts/link-issues.sh unsub   <parent> <child>
bash .github/scripts/link-issues.sh unblock <issue> <blocker>
bash .github/scripts/link-issues.sh show    <issue>

The script resolves issue numbers to GraphQL node IDs automatically, and treats "already linked" as a no-op so re-runs are safe.

docs.title: From Claude Code
docs.text:
The link-gh-issues skill (at .claude/skills/link-gh-issues/SKILL.md) guides Claude through the same operations — useful for bulk-applying relationships from a drafted wave backlog, parsing the Issues checklist out of a theme epic body, or verifying that the native links match the prose.

Example prompts:

  • "Apply the relationships from epic #29"
  • "Link #42, #43, #44 as sub-issues of #7"
  • "Mark #44 as blocked by #43"
  • "What's blocking #44?" (Claude runs make gh-show ISSUE=44 or the underlying GraphQL query)

docs.title: Raw GraphQL (for reference)
docs.text:
Under the hood the helper runs:

mutation { addSubIssue(input: { issueId: "<parent-node-id>", subIssueId: "<child-node-id>" }) { subIssue { number } } }
mutation { addBlockedBy(input: { issueId: "<this-node-id>", blockingIssueId: "<blocker-node-id>" }) { issue { number } } }

Issue node IDs are resolved via gh api repos/:owner/:repo/issues/<N> --jq .node_id.

docs.title: Operator parameter vocabulary
docs.text:
Every pipekit_ops.Operator constructor is keyword-only, and one concept has one parameter name across every family (dim, bands, window, size, fill_value, seed, …). The full table lives with the rest of the geotoolz package rules in packages/geotoolz-ops/AGENTS.md; tests/test_operator_contract.py::test_constructors_are_keyword_only and ::test_constructor_vocabulary enforce it.

Agents (and people) start from the root AGENTS.md: the package map, "reuse before you write", and the checklist below.

docs.title: Pre-commit checklist
docs.text:
Run these locally before opening a PR:

make format       # ruff format . + ruff check --fix .   (applies changes)
make lint         # ruff check .                         (CI-style check)
make typecheck    # ty check
make test         # pytest

Note that make format mutates files — it formats and applies autofixes. make lint is the CI-parity read-only check. Run make format first, commit the result, then run make lint / make test to verify.

Pre-commit hooks run ruff on every commit. Run make precommit to apply them to all files manually.

Commit messages follow the Conventional Commits specification — enforced on PR titles by .github/workflows/conventional-commits.yml.

docs.title: Bumping the pipekit pin
docs.text:
pipekit-ops (with pipekit-array and pipekit-train) is pulled from GitHub (not PyPI) and pinned to a release tag in the root pyproject.toml under [tool.uv.sources], so the Operator contract geotoolz is written against is the one that is installed and tested. To move it:

  1. Pick a pipekit release tag and set it as tag = "<tag>" on all three sources. They must share one tag: pipekit's packages point at each other at the same commit, so per-package tags make uv report conflicting URLs for pipekit-ops.
  2. Raise the pipekit-ops>=X.Y.Z floor in packages/geotoolz-array/pyproject.toml, packages/geotoolz-ops/pyproject.toml and packages/geotoolz-patcher/pyproject.toml (and the pipekit-array / pipekit-train floors) if the new release is required.
  3. Run uv lock --upgrade-package pipekit-ops, then the full pre-commit checklist.

docs.title: How the packages interlock
docs.text:
Each package works on its own; the seams between them are small, typed, first-class API — so a catalog query, a product reader, a patcher and an operator chain fit together without glue code.

Five packages, one job each, on one carrier (geotoolz-array's GeoArray). geotoolz-cloud sits underneath the others: every read or write that touches a bucket goes through it.

Step Package Hands the next step Find — which files cover my area and dates? geocatalog a GeoSlice query result, staged local files Read — open this mission's product geoproducts a geoarray.RasterSource / GeoArray Cut — make model-sized pieces and put them back geopatcher Patches, then a stitched GeoArray Compute — what do I do to each piece? geoops a GeoArray with the input's georeferencing Store — buckets, credentials, COGs geocloud pooled clients, files on disk, validated COGs

docs.title: The seams
docs.text:
1. GeoSlice — the catalog ↔ loader ↔ patcher request. A frozen (bounds, interval, resolution, crs) request for data. Catalogs answer it, loaders read it, and opt-in exact grid alignment (align=, count_steps, is_grid_aligned) keeps slice shapes honest across co-registered products.

2. geocatalog.patch.field_for — catalog rows become patcher fields. geocatalog.staging.stage copies remote assets into a local cache (through geocloud.files, the geotoolz-catalog[cloud] extra), and field_for mosaics the rows onto a GeoSlice grid — in the slice CRS, across files in any CRS — and wraps the result as one geopatcher.RasterField, so a query drops straight into SpatialPatcher.split / merge (geotoolz-catalog[patch]).

3. ProductReader — every reader is a geoarray.RasterSource. A geoproducts reader drops into geopatcher.RasterField or geoproducts.stack without adapters. A geotoolz operator needs pixels, so call reader.load() first. A sensor's presets bind geotoolz operators to its band names (geotoolz-products[operators]).

4. geoops.patch_ops — the patcher joins the operator graph. GridSampler → ApplyToChips → MergePatches (the same classes as geopatcher.integrations.pipekit) puts tile → predict → stitch inside a Sequential, and the label-aware StratifiedSample / BalancedSampler emit the same Patch carrier for training draws. See Tile → operate → stitch.

5. Coregistration operators plug into matched patching. geopatcher.matched.MatchedField fans one anchor out across sources and takes a coregistration callable per secondary — geoops.geom.coregister operators (RasterToRasterLike, RasterToPoints, …). The catalog's matchup engine finds the row pairs, the patcher reads them, the operators align them.

6. geocloud — one pool, one credential registry. geocloud.store owns the process-wide obstore client pool and geocloud.credentials the per-bucket credentials, so the catalog's staging, the patcher's CogField, the product readers' bucket helpers and geocloud.cog.write_cog share connections and grants: register a bucket once, then pass only URIs.

docs.title: All of them at once — methane screening with labels
docs.text:
A training-data and screening pass over the Permian Basin. Carbon Mapper (geoproducts) supplies the known methane sources; the catalog (geocatalog) finds the Sentinel-2 SWIR scenes; the patcher (geopatcher) tiles them; a geotoolz SWIR-ratio retrieval runs per tile; and the known sources are rasterized onto the very same grid as labels. The output is an aligned (score, labels) pair, ready to threshold, evaluate or train on.

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import planetary_computer
import pyproj
import pystac_client
from geoarray import GeoArray

import geocatalog as gc
import geopatcher as gp
import geoops as gz
from geoproducts import carbonmapper as cm
from geoops.patch_ops import ApplyToChips, GridSampler, MergePatches

bbox_lonlat: tuple[float, float, float, float] = (-104.2, 31.9, -103.9, 32.2)  # Delaware Basin
utm: str = "EPSG:32613"                                                         # UTM 13N, metres

# 1 · products — known oil & gas methane sources (Carbon Mapper, typed records)
config: cm.CarbonMapperConfig = cm.CarbonMapperConfig.load()   # ~/.geoproducts/auth_carbonmapper.json or env
token: str = config.get_token() or config.refresh_access_token()
sources: list[cm.CMSource] = cm.list_sources(token, bbox=bbox_lonlat, sectors=["1B2"])

# 2 · catalog — June 2025 Sentinel-2 SWIR bands on a 20 m UTM grid
aoi: gc.GeoSlice = gc.GeoSlice(
    bounds=pyproj.Transformer.from_crs("EPSG:4326", utm, always_xy=True).transform_bounds(*bbox_lonlat),
    interval=pd.Interval(pd.Timestamp("2025-06-01"), pd.Timestamp("2025-06-30"), closed="both"),
    resolution=(20.0, 20.0),                              # native SWIR → grid (H, W) = (1675, 1431)
    crs=utm,
)
client: pystac_client.Client = pystac_client.Client.open(
    "https://planetarycomputer.microsoft.com/api/stac/v1",
    modifier=planetary_computer.sign_inplace,
)
swir: dict[str, gp.RasterField] = {
    band: gc.patch.field_for(
        gc.staging.stage(
            gc.sources.from_stac_search(client, collections=["sentinel-2-l2a"], bounds=bbox_lonlat,
                                datetime="2025-06", asset_key=band),
            dest="./cache",
        ).query(aoi),
        aoi,
    )                                                    # (1, 1675, 1431) uint16 per band
    for band in ("B11", "B12")                           # SWIR-1 ≈ 1610 nm · SWIR-2 ≈ 2190 nm
}
scene: GeoArray = gz.StackBands()([swir["B11"].reader, swir["B12"].reader])  # (2, 1675, 1431) uint16

# 3 · patcher + operators — SWIR-ratio methane score, tile by tile
patcher: gp.SpatialPatcher = gp.SpatialPatcher(
    geometry=gp.spatial.geometry.Rectangular(size=(128, 128), boundary="pad"),
    sampler=gp.spatial.sampler.RegularStride(step=(96, 96)),
    window=gp.spatial.window.Hann(),
    aggregation=gp.spatial.aggregation.OverlapAdd(),
)
enhancement: gz.Sequential = (
    gz.DNToReflectance(scale=1e-4)                       # (2, h, w) uint16 → float64 reflectance
    | gz.SBMP(swir1=0, swir2=1)                          # (2, h, w) → (h, w) CH4 enhancement score
)
field: gp.RasterField = gp.RasterField(scene)
screen: gz.Sequential = gz.Sequential([
    GridSampler(patcher=patcher),                        # field → list[Patch]       (2, 128, 128) each
    ApplyToChips(operator=enhancement),                  # list[Patch] → list[Patch] (128, 128) each
    MergePatches(aggregation=gp.spatial.aggregation.OverlapAdd(), domain=field.domain),
])
score: GeoArray = screen(field)                        # (1675, 1431) float64, on the scene's grid

# 4 · products again — known sources rasterized onto the same grid as labels
labels: GeoArray = cm.rasterize_sources_like(sources, score, buffer_m=150.0)  # (1675, 1431) uint8 {0, 1}

pair: tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray] = (np.asarray(score), np.asarray(labels))  # aligned pixel-for-pixel

Swap one stage at a time: a MatchedFilter instead of SBMP, or cm.list_plumes instead of sources for event-level labels. Two swaps need one more step each:

  • A DuckDB catalog for 10⁶+ scenes. stage takes an in-memory catalog, so query the DuckDB catalog down to the AOI, then call .materialize().
  • Continent-scale outputs. OverlapAdd(streaming=True) writes to disk only with a target_path and chunks; see streaming overlap-add.

docs.title: geotoolz-array
docs.text: One georeferenced array for NumPy and JAX. A GeoArray holds the array, its affine transform, CRS, fill value and metadata, and knows which pixel sits where — imported as geoarray.

docs.title: Where it comes from
docs.text:
A raster is an array plus where its pixels are. Keep the two apart and every function has to carry both; keep them together by subclassing the array type, and the first operation from another array library loses the georeferencing. JAX arrays cannot be subclassed at all.

GeoArray holds its array instead, so one carrier works on NumPy and on JAX. It is a JAX pytree: the data and a float64 transform are leaves, which jit, grad and vmap trace, and the stored dims, coordinates, CRS, fill value and attrs are static. A new transform (another scene, another patch) reuses compiled code, and gradients reach the georeferencing.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
pip install geotoolz-array              # NumPy carriers, Grid, PixelWindow
pip install 'geotoolz-array[jax]'       # + JAX carriers and the pytree
pip install 'geotoolz-array[vector]'    # + footprint as a shapely polygon
pip install 'geotoolz-array[georeader]' # + GeoTensor <-> GeoArray
pip install 'geotoolz-array[xarray]'    # + to_xarray / from_xarray (CF spatial_ref)
Extra Pulls in Needed for (base) numpy, pyproj, affine, pipekit, pipekit-array GeoArray, GeoSwath, GeoPoints on NumPy data, geoarray.coords, geoarray.types, the dim-level functions, Grid, PixelWindow, FrozenAttrs [jax] jax JAX data, GeoArray.to_jax, jit / grad / vmap over carriers [vector] shapely footprint [georeader] georeader-spaceml geoarray.interop.georeader (from_georeader, to_georeader) [xarray] xarray to_xarray / from_xarray, to_dataset, to_datatree; readable types on DataArrays

A JAX carrier keeps its transform in float64, so it needs jax.config.update("jax_enable_x64", True). The data keeps its own dtype.

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text:
Wrap a Sentinel-2 chip in UTM 13N, read its grid, then move it to JAX and jit a function of it.

import jax
import numpy as np

from geoarray import GeoArray, Grid
from geoarray.coords import SpectralAxis

jax.config.update("jax_enable_x64", True)

# Shapes: C = 2 bands (B11, B12), H × W = 600 × 600 pixels of 20 m
chip: GeoArray = GeoArray(
    np.zeros((2, 600, 600), dtype=np.float32),  # (C, H, W) float32
    (20.0, 0.0, 600000.0, 0.0, -20.0, 3550000.0),  # (a, b, c, d, e, f)
    "EPSG:32613",
    fill_value=np.nan,
    dims=("band", "y", "x"),
    coords=(SpectralAxis(names=("B11", "B12"), wavelength_nm=(1610.0, 2190.0)),),
)
b12: GeoArray = chip.sel(band="B12")  # (H, W) float32: dims y x
grid: Grid = chip.grid  # transform, CRS, (600, 600)
grid.bounds  # (600000.0, 3538000.0, 612000.0, 3550000.0)

on_device: GeoArray = chip.to_jax()  # (C, H, W) float32 · transform float64
total = jax.jit(lambda g: g.data.sum())(on_device)  # () float32

Slice it, cut a window by map bounds, and crop patches inside vmap: each result carries the transform of the pixels it holds.

import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp
import numpy as np

from geoarray import GeoArray, PixelWindow, crop, read_window

jax.config.update("jax_enable_x64", True)

# Shapes: C = 2 bands, H × W = 600 × 600 pixels of 20 m
scene: GeoArray = GeoArray(
    np.zeros((2, 600, 600), dtype=np.float32),  # (C, H, W) float32
    (20.0, 0.0, 600000.0, 0.0, -20.0, 3550000.0),  # (a, b, c, d, e, f)
    "EPSG:32613",
    fill_value=np.nan,
    dims=("band", "y", "x"),
).to_jax()

sub: GeoArray = scene[..., 100:356, 200:456]  # (C, 256, 256): the origin moves
window: PixelWindow = scene.grid.window((604000.0, 3542880.0, 609120.0, 3548000.0))
same: GeoArray = read_window(scene, window)  # the same pixels as sub

offsets = jnp.array([[0, 0], [256, 256], [344, 344]])  # (N, 2) int
patches: GeoArray = jax.jit(jax.vmap(lambda o: crop(scene, o, (256, 256))))(offsets)
patches.batch_shape  # (3,): (N, C, 256, 256) data, one (6,) transform per patch
valid = scene.valid_mask()  # (H, W) bool: every band finite and not the fill

docs.title: Backends and georeader
docs.text:
NumPy and JAX carriers mix eagerly, as NumPy and jnp arrays do. Inside jit, grad or vmap the data are tracers, and NumPy code on them raises GeoArrayTraceError instead of JAX's generic error.

Call NumPy carrier JAX carrier np.asarray(g) the data, no copy a host copy; raises under a trace; warns with set_options(warn_on_transfer=True) combine, stack, concatenate, write_window with mixed inputs — NumPy inputs move to JAX (needs x64) from_georeader(gt) / to_georeader(g) GeoTensor ↔ GeoArray, sharing memory to_georeader needs g.to_numpy() first 
import numpy as np
from affine import Affine
from georeader.geotensor import GeoTensor

from geoarray import GeoArray
from geoarray.interop.georeader import from_georeader, to_georeader

gt: GeoTensor = GeoTensor(
    np.zeros((2, 600, 600), dtype=np.float32),  # (C, H, W) float32
    Affine(20.0, 0.0, 600000.0, 0.0, -20.0, 3550000.0),
    "EPSG:32613",
    fill_value_default=np.nan,
)
g: GeoArray = from_georeader(gt)  # (C, H, W) float32, the same memory
back: GeoTensor = to_georeader(g[..., :256, :256])  # (C, 256, 256), origin kept

docs.title: What's inside
docs.text: Name Use it to… Guide GeoArray carry data with its stored dims, coordinates, transform, CRS, fill value and attrs; sel / isel by name, grid, with_data, to_jax, to_numpy, from_coords Concepts GeoSwath, GeoPoints, pad_points carry swaths in sensor geometry (lat/lon leaves) and point sets (xy, z, time, valid) Tutorial geoarray.coords say what a dim means: SpectralAxis, VariableAxis, VerticalAxis, TimeAxis, PixelGrid, … Reference geoarray.types name common shapes (GeoImage, GeoMapSeries, GeoTracks, …) and check them with check_dims Reference isel, sel, reduce, map_over, concat, combine, … pipekit-array's dim-level functions, on every named carrier; a pipekit-array KernelOp runs on carriers too Concepts to_pixel map coordinates to fractional pixels (functax's kernel, re-exported); H(x) itself is geoops.geom.interp_at When to jit to_xarray, from_xarray, to_dataset, to_datatree cross to xarray losslessly ([xarray]) Cross to xarray Grid describe a pixel grid without data: bounds, res, shift, crop, from_bounds, isclose, get_config Reference PixelWindow name a rectangle of pixels, rasterio's Window without rasterio; Grid.window / Grid.bounds_of convert to and from map bounds Reference g[...], isel slice with the transform following; select bands with their per-band attrs Reference map, shift_origin, squeeze, expand_dims change the data on the same grid, move the georeferencing, add or drop leading axes Reference crop, read_window, write_window, pad cut, read past the edges, write and pad pixels; crop inside jit / vmap Reference valid_mask, pixel_coords, footprint find the pixels that hold data, their map coordinates, the outline ([vector]) Reference stack, concatenate join carriers that share a grid (stack(gs, "time"); concatenate is concat by position) Reference FrozenAttrs keep metadata hashable, so it can key a compiled function Reference RasterSource, AsyncRasterSource describe a lazy reader: its grid, and reads that return a GeoArray (read_window, load); a GeoArray is one Reference set_options, get_options, HostTransferWarning find the NumPy steps that copy JAX data to the host Reference from_georeader, to_georeader bridge to georeader's GeoTensor, zero-copy, and (source_from_georeader / source_to_georeader) its lazy readers ([georeader]) Reference as_transform, as_crs coerce an affine.Affine, six numbers, an EPSG code or WKT Reference
